title: UK's New PM Burnham Scraps VAT on Electricity Bills in First Policy Move
excerpt: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the removal of value-added tax from domestic electricity bills starting October 1, saving households around £45 a year in his first major policy action.
body:
• Prime Minister Andy Burnham will remove the 5% VAT from domestic electricity bills starting October 1, saving households around £45 per year.
  • The £850 million cost will be funded by cancelling the government's £1.8 billion digital ID programme, which a cross-party committee had called a "fiasco."
  • A Keir Starmer ally challenged the funding plan, warning the digital ID scheme was itself unfunded and the government would need to explain how it would pay at the budget.
  • Burnham is also considering cutting bus fares and introducing rent controls as part of broader cost-of-living measures.

VAT Removed From Electricity Bills

On his second day in office, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that his government would remove the value-added tax from domestic electricity bills from October 1. The move will cut the current 5 percent VAT rate to zero, saving the average household approximately £45 on an annual bill of around £1,862.

https://x.com/ARISEtv/status/2079471983121641758

The measure is expected to cost the Treasury around £850 million in the 2026-27 financial year. Burnham said it would be funded by savings from the cancellation of the government's £1.8 billion digital ID programme — a plan for all employees to hold a digital identity document that a cross-party committee of lawmakers had described as a "fiasco."

"Westminster has not been working for people for too long, with families struggling with the cost of living. That needs to change. I said I wanted to give people breathing space, and that's what I'm announcing on my second day as Prime Minister."

— Andy Burnham, UK Prime Minister

Markets and Critics Watch Closely

Bond investors reacted cautiously to the announcement, watching closely for how the new government plans to finance its support measures. Borrowing costs rose on Monday, the day Burnham took office, though government borrowing figures for June came in slightly below official forecasts at £16 billion — offering some early respite.

Darren Jones, an ally of former Prime Minister Keir Starmer and ex-Cabinet Minister, questioned whether the funding plan held up, arguing that the digital ID scheme was itself unfunded.

"The government will have to set out how it will pay for its new policies at the budget."

— Darren Jones, Former Cabinet Minister

Chancellor John Healey, Burnham's unexpected pick for the Treasury, defended the move, saying it would "give families some breathing room on bills" while helping to bring down inflation. Energy firms are expected to pass the VAT cut on to consumers.

Broader Cost-of-Living Agenda

The VAT cut comes on top of a £150 reduction to energy bills introduced at the last Budget. With energy prices expected to rise again later in the year due to the ongoing Middle East conflict, Burnham has signalled that further measures are under consideration.

Among the policies being weighed are reinstating the £2 cap on bus fares — raised to £3 by the previous government — and introducing rent controls. Burnham said on Monday that his early policies might not "take all of the pressure off" but that a longer-term plan would be set out later in the year at the Budget.

"Prime Minister Andy Burnham will remove the 5% VAT from domestic electricity bills starting October 1, saving households around £45 per year."

What It Means for NRI Families

The UK's 1.8 million-strong Indian diaspora community stands to benefit directly from the electricity bill reduction. Indian families in Britain — many of whom run small businesses, restaurants or corner shops with high energy usage — have been among those hardest hit by rising utility costs in recent years.

Burnham, a 56-year-old former Mayor of Greater Manchester who built his political career on cost-of-living issues, has positioned himself as a leader focused on practical relief rather than ideological shifts. His early moves suggest he intends to prioritise household finances and demonstrate that, as he put it, he is "serious about helping them out."
